# Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML {#sec-data-efficiency}

**Under the frozen comparison protocol ISLA appeared 2.8x more accurate
than GeoTransolver and plain Transolver from 35 high-lift training cases;
the protocol fed the baselines the freestream as a physical velocity of
2,679.5 in/s while ISLA received a unit direction, and when the baselines
are retrained with the unit direction and nothing else changed they are
1.1–1.25x more accurate than ISLA (1.07–1.11x against the weights-off
ablation, which is not adopted).** The first section states the protocol,
the second reports the control that found the artifact
(@sec-de-unit-drive), and the remaining sections report the physical-drive
ladder as the measurement it is: the 2.8x, the 2.2x at 210 cases, the
paired per-case counts, the unseen-geometry factors, the fixed-angle figure
and the force-coefficient errors are all against physical-drive baselines,
and their unit-drive counterparts above 35 cases are training
(@sec-program-status; prediction written before the rerun: the baselines
match or beat ISLA at every rung). On DrivAerML, where the freestream is fixed
and GeoTransolver also received the physical velocity, GeoTransolver is
1.2–1.3x more accurate than ISLA from 27 training cases up
(@sec-de-drivaerml), a lower bound on its lead. Every ratio between
architectures in this chapter is the baseline's error divided by ISLA's, so a
value above one favours ISLA. The chapter's limits are stated in
@sec-de-limits and collected with the rest of the book's in @sec-limits.

## What was measured {#sec-de-setup}

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-datasets) holds 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing
geometries, each simulated at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°. Its
curated data-efficiency splits are nested — 35 training cases inside 210
inside 510 inside 1,260 — and all four share one 180-case validation set
and one sealed 360-case test set (@sec-splits). The training subsets are
random draws from the 1,260-case pool, so the 35-case split contains 3–7
cases at each angle except 18°, of which it has none, and 33 distinct
geometries.

The quantity reported is the relative L2 error of surface pressure on the
validation cases (@sec-metrics): for one case, the norm of the error over
its 10,000 sampled surface points divided by the norm of the true field on
the same points, then the arithmetic mean over the 180 cases. Every
architecture is trained under the same frozen protocol (@sec-protocol):
10,000 sampled surface points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no
augmentation, two seeds, and the learning rate each architecture prefers
on the full split (1e-3 for ISLA and GeoTransolver; Transolver, which had
no prior tuning on this dataset, was run at 1e-3 and 3e-3 and is reported
at the better of the two per rung, 3e-3). The final-epoch checkpoint of each
run is evaluated; no checkpoint is selected on validation error. The
validation set was used for the learning-rate choice on the full split, for
Transolver's learning-rate choice per small-data rung, and, as in any
sequential program, by the ablations designed after earlier readouts and by
the selection of which results to present (@sec-de-limits). Resources are
matched in parameters (8.9M for ISLA against 9.0M
for GeoTransolver and 6.0M for Transolver) and tokens per case; on
one GPU and one instrument, peak training memory at this token count is
1.6 GiB for ISLA's current code against 4.1 GiB for GeoTransolver, while
the ISLA code that trained these checkpoints peaked at 9.3 GiB, and ISLA's
step is 3.7x slower (@sec-resource-matching). The
baselines received the freestream as a physical velocity and ISLA as a unit
direction; @sec-de-unit-drive measures what that asymmetry did. The test
split was never read by any model in this chapter; every number in it is a
validation-set number.

## The input-scale control {#sec-de-unit-drive}

**Retrained with the unit freestream direction in place of the physical
velocity, and nothing else changed, GeoTransolver's 35-case error falls
from 0.381 to 0.124 and Transolver's from 0.404 to 0.115, below ISLA's
0.138.** The recipe nondimensionalizes the surface fields and the
coordinates but not the freestream vector it hands each model as a global
input: GeoTransolver's context projector and Transolver's per-token feature
concatenation received (2,679.5, 0, 0) in/s rotated by the angle of attack,
while ISLA's drive input is the unit direction by construction. At that
magnitude GeoTransolver's untrained global-context projector assigns every
head to a single slice, where at unit magnitude it spreads over about 200 of
256 (@sec-part-baseline). The control, preregistered with bars before launch
(@sec-nb-udrv-prereg), is the frozen 35-case protocol with one hydra override
per baseline (`forward_kwargs.global_embedding=global_data.U_inf_dir` for
GeoTransolver, `forward_kwargs.fx.source=global_data.U_inf_dir` for
Transolver), the declared learning rates (1e-3 and 3e-3), seeds 42 and 43,
evaluated on the same 180 validation cases by the same inference path.
Third seeds and the learning-rate steel-men that the physical-drive
baselines had received were then run for the unit-drive baselines
(@sec-nb-wave3-35-verdict): the third seeds move neither mean by more than
0.001; GeoTransolver at 3e-3 improves to 0.111 (two seeds 0.112 / 0.109;
lower than its 1e-3 lane on 158 of 180 cases), so by the protocol's
best-rate rule GeoTransolver's 35-case number is 0.111; Transolver at 1e-3
is worse (0.127) and stays at 3e-3. The weights-off ablation of ISLA
(@sec-mechanism), a discretization-dependent configuration that the program
measures but does not adopt (@sec-principle), scores 0.123 on three seeds.

| Model, 35 training cases | Freestream input | Pressure | Velocity | Wall shear | Cases where the baseline beats ISLA | Geometries (of 118) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GeoTransolver | physical velocity (three seeds) | 0.381 | 0.342 | 0.564 | 0 of 180 | 0 |
| GeoTransolver | unit direction, lr 1e-3 (three seeds: 0.124, 0.125, 0.122) | **0.124** | **0.145** | **0.229** | 130 of 180 | 84 |
| GeoTransolver | unit direction, lr 3e-3 (two seeds: 0.112, 0.109) | **0.111** | **0.136** | **0.210** | 158 of 180 vs its 1e-3 lane | — |
| Transolver | physical velocity (three seeds) | 0.404 | 0.372 | 0.602 | 0 of 180 | 0 |
| Transolver | unit direction, lr 3e-3 (three seeds: 0.117, 0.113, 0.114) | **0.115** | **0.141** | **0.217** | 152 of 180 | 102 |
| Transolver | unit direction, lr 1e-3 (two seeds: 0.124, 0.129) | 0.127 | 0.148 | 0.234 | — | — |
| GeoTransolver | unit direction, lr 3e-3, measure-weighted slice pooling (three seeds: 0.113, 0.122, 0.117; float32) | **0.117** | — | — | — | — |
| Transolver | unit direction, lr 3e-3, measure-weighted slice pooling (three seeds: 0.121, 0.121, 0.123; float32) | **0.122** | — | — | — | — |
| ISLA | unit direction, measure weights on (three seeds) | 0.138 | 0.168 | 0.256 | — | — |
| ISLA | unit direction, measure weights off (three seeds: 0.121, 0.123, 0.124) | **0.123** | **0.152** | **0.234** | — | — |

: The unit-drive control at 35 training cases. Relative L2 on the 180
shared validation cases, seed means (bfloat16 evaluation; the float32
re-evaluation of all 22 checkpoints agrees with every entry to the third
decimal and leaves every ratio unchanged, @sec-nb-fp32-35-regrade); the paired counts use seed-mean errors
per case (sign test p = 2 × 10⁻⁹ for GeoTransolver, 8 × 10⁻²² for
Transolver; median ISLA ÷ baseline ratio 1.09 and 1.17). Each unit-drive
baseline beats its physical-drive self on 180 of 180 cases (median 3.4x and
3.8x). Data: results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json. {#tbl-unit-drive}

The two measure-weighted rows are the baselines with the same quadrature
measure ISLA carries in their slice pooling (@sec-nb-mw-verdict): they pay
6.5% for it at this rung and remain 0.85x and 0.88x of ISLA's error, so
about a third of the baselines' lead here was the sampling density they
read and two thirds was not; on DrivAerML the same change costs nothing
(@sec-consistency-bench). The preregistered bar for "the drive scale
carries a material part of the deficit" was a unit-drive error of 0.27 or
below for GeoTransolver and 0.29 for Transolver; both land at less than half of it, and below ISLA. The
reading is direct: the baselines' small-data deficit on HiLiftAeroML was the
input scale, not the architecture, and the steel-man controls of
@sec-de-controls (a higher learning rate, doubled epochs, a third seed, the
same attention family without a geometry encoder) could not find it because
each kept the input. With the artifact removed, GeoTransolver and Transolver
are 1.1x and 1.2x more accurate than ISLA at 35 cases on every field, and
plain Transolver, the smaller and simpler model, is the most accurate of the
three. The ratios that follow in this chapter are therefore not comparisons
between architectures; they are the record of a protocol and of how it was
corrected. The unit-drive baselines were then run at 210 cases, at 4 and 21
training geometries and at the fixed angle under the same control
(@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg), with the prediction, written first, that they match
or beat ISLA at every rung. They do. At 210 cases GeoTransolver fed the unit
direction scores 0.0539 in float32 on three seeds (0.0532 / 0.0535 / 0.0550)
against ISLA's 0.0643 on three seeds, 0.84x and lower on 161 of 180
validation cases, and Transolver at its better rate 0.0578 (0.0582 / 0.0582 /
0.0569), 0.90x and lower on 149 of 180; the
physical-drive GeoTransolver's 0.141 on the same cases, the 2.2x of the
ladder, is 3.4x worse than its unit-drive self on 178 of 180 cases
(`results/udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json`, @sec-nb-udrvl-210-verdict). The weights-off
ablation of ISLA at this rung scores 0.0589 in float32, 0.92x of the
weighted model and lower on 150 of 180 cases, which prices the measure
semantics at 8% here; it remains behind the unit-drive GeoTransolver (0.91x
of it) and at parity with Transolver (0.99x), and is not adopted
(@sec-principle, @sec-nb-nowl-210-verdict). The other rungs are reported in
their sections below; only the 1,260-case rerun is still training. The fair-comparison protocol now requires every architecture to
receive the freestream at unit scale (@sec-protocol).

How much of this ordering belongs to the particular 35 cases? The 35-case
split is one random draw from the 1,260-case pool, and every number above is
a seed mean on that draw. The cross-dataset companion program re-ran the four
unit-drive arms (GeoTransolver and Transolver at their best rates, ISLA with
measure weights on and off) on three further geometry-stratified 35-case
draws, three seeds each, evaluated in float32 (`research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json`).
The ordering holds on every draw. GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA is 0.881, 0.892 and
0.957 on the three new draws against 0.895 on the draw above (mean 0.910, 90%
interval 0.84–0.98); Transolver ÷ ISLA is 0.846, 0.852 and 0.900 against 0.829
(mean 0.866, interval 0.82–0.92); weights-off ISLA ÷ ISLA is 0.896, 0.898 and
0.947 against 0.885 (mean 0.914, interval 0.87–0.96), so the weights-off gain
at 35 cases is 5–10% and draw-dependent. The draw in @tbl-unit-drive is
typical for every arm, at the easy end of the range. The number that changes
practice is the variance decomposition: the between-draw standard deviation of
an arm's error is 8.8 (GeoTransolver), 10.9 (Transolver), 3.4 (ISLA, whose
seed spread is two to three times the others') and 8.4 (weights-off ISLA)
times its between-seed standard deviation, and the hardest draw is 24% harder
than the easiest for GeoTransolver. A two-seed number at this rung therefore
understates its uncertainty by a factor of 3–11; read the 35-case ratios in
this book with the intervals above, not with their seed spreads, and expect
future rungs to be run over draws rather than seeds. The 210-case rung was
then run the same way (three geometry-stratified draws, three seeds each,
float32; `research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json`): GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA is 0.869, 0.907 and 0.843
across the draws (curated 0.838; mean 0.873, 90% interval 0.82–0.93),
Transolver ÷ ISLA 0.893, 0.936 and 0.880 (curated 0.898; mean 0.903,
0.85–0.95), and the weights-off ablation ÷ ISLA 0.932, 0.920 and 0.902
(mean 0.918, 0.89–0.94), so both "ISLA behind" orderings stand with
intervals about half as wide as at 35 cases, the measure semantics cost a
stable 8% on every draw where the cost was draw-dependent at 35, and the two
baselines trade places with data: GeoTransolver's lead grows from 35 to 210
cases (0.91 to 0.87) while Transolver's shrinks (0.87 to 0.90). The
between-draw to within-draw spread ratio falls to 1.8–3.1 for ISLA and
GeoTransolver (7.6 for Transolver, whose seeds nearly coincide), and the
curated draw is typical for every arm but GeoTransolver, for which it is
the easiest of the four.

## The result under the physical-drive protocol {#sec-de-result}

The figure and tables of this section are the ladder as it was run, with
the baselines fed the physical freestream velocity. Read them as
measurements of that protocol, not as the standing of the architectures;
the standing at 35 cases is @tbl-unit-drive, and above 35 cases it is not
yet measured.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-data-efficiency
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Surface-pressure relative L2 error on the shared 180-case validation set
#|   versus number of training cases, for GeoTransolver (red circles),
#|   ISLA (blue squares) and plain Transolver without a geometry
#|   encoder (grey triangles, dashed; at its better learning rate, 3e-3).
#|   Lines join seed means, shaded bands span the seeds (three at 35 and 210
#|   cases, two at 1,260), small dots are the individual seeds. The annotated factors are each baseline's error
#|   divided by ISLA's at the same rung (above one favours ISLA); they are
#|   against physical-drive baselines, which received the freestream as a
#|   physical velocity where ISLA received a unit direction (see @sec-de-unit-drive). Protocol: 10,000 sampled surface
#|   points per case, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation, learning rate
#|   1e-3 for GeoTransolver and ISLA; ISLA in its constant-gauge
#|   configuration. The figure does not show scaling beyond 1,260 cases and does not show
#|   DrivAerML, where the ordering reverses (@tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder). Data:
#|   results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json,
#|   results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json,
#|   results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json (third seeds).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
data = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi, pts = [], [], [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(a=arch, s=s) in lad]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); lo.append(min(v)); hi.append(max(v)); pts.append(v)
    data[arch] = (xs, means, lo, hi, pts)
xs, means, lo, hi, pts = [], [], [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = None
    for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3"):
        v = [t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(lr=lr, s=s) in t1]
        if len(v) >= 2 and (best is None or statistics.mean(v) < statistics.mean(best)):
            best = v
    xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(best)); lo.append(min(best)); hi.append(max(best)); pts.append(best)
data["t"] = (xs, means, lo, hi, pts)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 5.0))
style = {"gt": (RED, "o", "-", 2.2), "t": (GREY, "^", "--", 1.6), "mt2": (BLUE, "s", "-", 2.2)}
for arch in ("gt", "t", "mt2"):
    xs, means, lo, hi, pts = data[arch]; c, mk, ls, lw = style[arch]
    ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color=c, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=lw, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
    for x, v in zip(xs, pts):
        ax.scatter([x] * len(v), v, color=c, s=14, alpha=0.9, zorder=4)
ax.annotate("GeoTransolver", (35, data["gt"][1][0]), xytext=(14, 2), textcoords="offset points", color=RED, fontweight="bold", va="center",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
ax.annotate("ISLA", (210, data["mt2"][1][1]), xytext=(14, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=BLUE, fontweight="bold", va="center",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
xm, ym = (35 * 210) ** 0.5, (data["t"][1][0] * data["t"][1][1]) ** 0.5
ax.annotate("Transolver", (xm, ym), xytext=(-3, -7), textcoords="offset points", color=GREY, fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="top",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
for i, n in enumerate((35, 210)):
    r_gt = data["gt"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]; r_t = data["t"][1][i] / data["mt2"][1][i]
    ymid = (data["gt"][1][i] * data["mt2"][1][i]) ** 0.5
    ax.annotate("", (n, data["mt2"][1][i]), (n, data["gt"][1][i]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=INK2, lw=0.9, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=4))
    ax.text(n * 1.08, ymid, f"GeoTransolver {r_gt:.1f}x ISLA\nTransolver {r_t:.1f}x ISLA", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="center", linespacing=1.3,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
r_full = data["gt"][1][2] / data["mt2"][1][2]
ax.annotate(f"{r_full:.2f}x (parity)", (1260, (data["gt"][1][2] * data["mt2"][1][2]) ** 0.5), xytext=(14, 30), textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260"])
ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.04", "0.06", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"])
ax.set_xlim(22, 3200)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Surface pressure error, rel-L2 [–]", color=INK2)
ax.set_title("Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML (shared 180-case validation set)", color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=11, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
inv = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "inv_transplant_2026-09-07.json"))
def pair(d, pat):
    v = [d[pat.format(s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(s=s) in d]
    return v
rows = []
for n, gpat, mpat, tpat in [(35, "lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}", "lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed{s}", "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}"),
                            (210, "lad_hl_gt_scarce_seed{s}", "lad_hl_mt2_scarce_seed{s}", "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}"),
                            (1260, "gt_hl_lr1_seed{s}", "mt2_hl_lr1_seed{s}", None)]:
    g, m = pair(lad, gpat), pair(lad, mpat)
    t = pair(t1, tpat) if tpat else []
    gm, mm = statistics.mean(g), statistics.mean(m)
    tcell = f"{statistics.mean(t):.3f} ({min(t):.3f}–{max(t):.3f})" if t else "—"
    tr = f"{statistics.mean(t)/mm:.1f}" if t else "—"
    rows.append(f"| {n:,} | {gm:.3f} ({min(g):.3f}–{max(g):.3f}) | {tcell} | **{mm:.3f}** ({min(m):.3f}–{max(m):.3f}) | {gm/mm:.2f} | {tr} |")
print("| training cases | GeoTransolver | Transolver (lr 3e-3) | ISLA | GT / ISLA | T / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
print("\n".join(rows))
print()
print(": Surface-pressure relative L2 error on the shared 180-case validation set: seed mean (seed range) for each architecture at each rung, and the ratio of each baseline's mean to ISLA's. Ratios above 1 mean ISLA is more accurate, against physical-drive baselines; see @sec-de-unit-drive. Same protocol and sources as @fig-hilift-data-efficiency. {#tbl-hilift-ladder}")
```

Two features of the numbers matter before any interpretation. The seed
spreads are small against the gaps at 35 and 210 cases (0.006 for ISLA and
0.035 for GeoTransolver against a gap of 0.25 at 35 cases), and the gap
closes monotonically with data under the physical drive: 2.8x, then 2.2x,
then parity. The 510-case rung fills the ladder's gap: ISLA scores 0.0495 (seeds
0.0486 / 0.0504), so its curve runs 0.138 → 0.065 → 0.0495 → 0.041 with
log-log slopes 0.42, 0.31 and 0.21 over the three segments, flattening
steadily; the physical-drive GeoTransolver scores 0.0568 there (seeds
0.061 / 0.053; 1.15x, ISLA lower on 156 of 180 cases) and the
physical-drive Transolver 0.0656 at either learning rate (1.33x; 170 of
180), both physical-drive measurements (results/w2_medium_reduction_2026-09-09.json;
@sec-nb-w2-medium-verdict). Their unit-drive counterparts reverse the
ordering, as at every other rung: unit-drive GeoTransolver scores 0.0410
(seeds 0.0418 / 0.0402), 0.84x of ISLA and lower on 168 of 180 cases, and
unit-drive Transolver 0.0441 (0.0437 / 0.0444), 0.90x and lower on 168 of
180, in float32 against the same ISLA checkpoints scored in float32 (0.0489;
@sec-nb-udrvl-510-verdict; results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json).
Along the case ladder the unit-drive ratio is flat, GeoTransolver 0.80x,
0.83x, 0.84x and Transolver 0.83x, 0.91x, 0.90x at 35, 210 and 510 cases.

The same-family control, also fed the physical velocity, shows that the
two baselines shared the collapse. Plain Transolver — GeoTransolver's
attention family without the geometry encoder — collapses exactly like
GeoTransolver at 35 cases (0.40, 2.9x ISLA), which is what a shared
mis-scaled input predicts (@sec-de-unit-drive), but recovers faster,
reaching 0.086 at 210 cases, where it is 1.8x more accurate than
GeoTransolver itself. So at 210 cases most of the 2.2x gap to
GeoTransolver is GeoTransolver falling behind its own backbone under the
same input, and ISLA's margin over the *better* physical-drive baseline is
1.3x. At 35 cases the two baselines are indistinguishable and the 2.8x
holds against both. Every statement of a physical-drive ratio in this book
carries both margins, because a headline built on the weaker baseline
overstates the difference.

**The horizontal reading is the one a practitioner would use, and under
the physical-drive protocol it reads as follows.** A ratio at a fixed
number of cases is the instrument reading; the engineering question is how
many CFD runs each architecture needs to reach a given error. Reading
@fig-hilift-data-efficiency horizontally:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-data-multiplier
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, math, statistics
from pathlib import Path
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
w2 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json"))["runs"]
lad = {**lad, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("lad_hl_")}}
t1 = {**t1, **{k: v for k, v in w2.items() if k.startswith("t1_hl_transolver")}}
def mean_of(d, pat):
    return statistics.mean(d[pat.format(s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43, 44) if pat.format(s=s) in d)
isla35, isla210 = mean_of(lad, "lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed{s}"), mean_of(lad, "lad_hl_mt2_scarce_seed{s}")
gt210 = mean_of(lad, "lad_hl_gt_scarce_seed{s}")
t210 = mean_of(t1, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}")
# ISLA's measured 35->210 segment as a power law: cases needed to reach a target error.
slope = math.log(isla35 / isla210) / math.log(210 / 35)
def isla_cases_for(err):
    return 35 * (isla35 / err) ** (1 / slope)
n_t = isla_cases_for(t210)
print("| target error (pressure rel-L2) | reached by | at cases | ISLA reaches it at | data multiplier |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
print(f"| {gt210:.3f} | GeoTransolver | 210 | 35 (measured: {isla35:.3f}) | **{210/35:.0f}x** |")
print(f"| {t210:.3f} | Transolver (lr 3e-3) | 210 | about {n_t:.0f} (interpolated on ISLA's 35→210 segment, slope {slope:.2f}) | **{210/n_t:.1f}x** |")
print(f"| {mean_of(lad, 'gt_hl_lr1_seed{s}'):.3f} | GeoTransolver | 1,260 | 1,260 (measured: {mean_of(lad, 'mt2_hl_lr1_seed{s}'):.3f}) | 1x |")
print()
print(": The data multiplier: how many more training cases each baseline needs than ISLA to reach the same surface-pressure error on the shared validation set, against physical-drive baselines; see @sec-de-unit-drive. The GeoTransolver row is two measured points (GeoTransolver at 210 cases against ISLA at 35); the Transolver row interpolates ISLA's case count on its own measured 35→210 power-law segment, so it is a reading of the curve, not a measured rung; the 1,260-case row is parity. Same protocol and sources as @tbl-hilift-ladder. {#tbl-data-multiplier}")
```

Stated this way, the physical-drive gap is a six-fold difference in CFD
runs at the 0.14 error level against GeoTransolver, about two-fold against
plain Transolver at the 0.09 level, and nothing at 1,260 cases. At 35 cases
the unit-drive control removes the gap outright (@tbl-unit-drive), so the
six-fold multiplier is a property of the protocol, not of the
architectures; whether any multiplier remains at the 0.09 level is what
the unit-drive 210-case rung decides. The multiplier falls as the target
error falls, which is the shape of the curves in
@fig-hilift-data-efficiency and the reason the book calls this a
data-efficiency measurement and not a scaling law (@sec-de-limits).

## The physical-drive gap case by case {#sec-de-paired}

The 180 validation cases are shared, so each can be scored once as a
paired comparison: for every case, each architecture's two-seed mean error
(@sec-metrics). The table reports, against the physical-drive baselines,
how many of the 180 cases ISLA wins, how many it wins on both seeds
individually (a stricter count), an exact two-sided sign test on n = 180,
and the distribution of the per-case error ratio. The same instrument
applied to the unit-drive baselines at 35 cases reverses the count: the
baselines win 130 and 152 of 180 (@tbl-unit-drive).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-paired
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
ps = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07.json"))
names = {"gt": "GeoTransolver", "transolver": "Transolver (lr 3e-3)"}
print("| training cases | baseline | cases ISLA wins (of 180) | wins on both seeds | sign-test p (n = 180) | median ratio (baseline / ISLA) | 10th–90th percentile |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n in ("35", "210", "1260"):
    for b in ("gt", "transolver"):
        k = f"mt2_vs_{b}"
        if k not in ps[n]:
            continue
        r = ps[n][k]
        print(f"| {int(n):,} | {names[b]} | **{r['mt2_wins_seed_mean']} / {r['n_cases']}** | {r['mt2_wins_both_seeds']} | {r['sign_test_p_n180']:.0e} | {r['median_ratio_base_over_mt2']:.2f} | {r['q10_ratio']:.2f}–{r['q90_ratio']:.2f} |")
print()
print(": Case-level paired comparison on the 180 shared validation cases. Each case is scored once by each architecture's two-seed mean pressure error; 'wins' counts cases where ISLA's error is lower, and the next column counts cases where ISLA is lower on each seed separately. The sign test is exact and two-sided against a 50% null on n = 180. Ratios are baseline error over ISLA error; above 1 favours ISLA, against physical-drive baselines; see @sec-de-unit-drive. Data: results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07.json. {#tbl-hilift-paired}")
```

At 35 cases there is no validation case, on either seed, where either
physical-drive baseline beats ISLA, and the worst tenth of cases still
favour ISLA by 1.8x. The 180 cases are drawn from 118 geometries, so they
are not 180 independent geometry replications; a 180-of-180 ordering
survives any grouping of the cases, but the p-values in the table are
case-level and read as such. At 210 cases ISLA wins 177 of 180 cases
against physical-drive GeoTransolver (175 on both seeds) and 165 of 180
against physical-drive Transolver (median 1.5x). At 1,260 cases, where the
means are at parity, ISLA is lower on 130 of 180 cases (103 on both seeds)
with a median ratio of 1.06 — a small per-case edge over the physical-drive
GeoTransolver that the mean comparison hides; whether it survives the unit
drive is a question for the 1,260-case rerun, and the paired view is the
instrument that will see it.

The same per-case errors answer a second question: do the two architectures
agree on *which* cases are hard? @tbl-hilift-percase-rho gives the Spearman
rank correlation between ISLA's and GeoTransolver's per-case errors at each
rung, next to each architecture's rank correlation with its own second seed,
which is the ceiling a correlation between two models could reach.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-percase-rho
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
hl = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json"))
dr = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json"))
print("| dataset and rung | cases | ρ ISLA vs GeoTransolver | ρ GeoTransolver, seed vs seed | ρ ISLA, seed vs seed | per-case ratio GeoTransolver / ISLA, 10th / 50th / 90th pct |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for key, label in (("35", "HiLiftAeroML, 35"), ("210", "HiLiftAeroML, 210"), ("1260", "HiLiftAeroML, 1,260"), ("single12", "HiLiftAeroML, single angle, 126 (18 held-out geometries)")):
    r = hl[key]; p = r["ratio_gt_over_isla_p10_p50_p90"]
    print(f"| {label} | {r['n']} | **{r['rho_isla_vs_gt']:.2f}** | {r['rho_gt_self']:.2f} | {r['rho_isla_self']:.2f} | {p[0]:.2f} / {p[1]:.2f} / {p[2]:.2f} |")
for s in ("45", "46"):
    r = dr[s]; p = [1 / x for x in reversed(r["ratio_p10_p50_p90"])]
    print(f"| DrivAerML, 435 (seed pair {s}) | {r['n']} | **{r['spearman_isla_vs_gt_per_case_pressure_l2']:.2f}** | {dr['self_consistency']['gt_seed45_vs_46']:.2f} | {dr['self_consistency']['isla_seed45_vs_46']:.2f} | {p[0]:.2f} / {p[1]:.2f} / {p[2]:.2f} |")
print()
print(": Do the architectures agree on which cases are hard? Spearman rank correlation of per-case surface-pressure error between ISLA and GeoTransolver (two-seed means per case on HiLiftAeroML; single seeds on DrivAerML, where the same-numbered seeds are paired), against each architecture's correlation with its own other seed. Ratios are GeoTransolver error over ISLA error per case (above 1 favours ISLA); GeoTransolver is the physical-drive model on both datasets (see @sec-de-unit-drive); on DrivAerML the artifact stores ISLA/GeoTransolver and the table inverts it. Data: results/hilift_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json, results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json. {#tbl-hilift-percase-rho}")
```

Each architecture is consistent with itself (0.87–0.97 across seeds), so the
cross-architecture correlations are resolved. At 35 and 210 cases they are
0.57 and 0.64, and the per-case ratio spans 1.8x to 4.6x; at 1,260 cases
the two orderings coincide (0.94, the seed ceiling) and the ratio collapses
to 0.92–1.18. On DrivAerML the orderings coincide at every size (0.86–0.89)
and GeoTransolver's edge is a near-constant factor. The reason the
orderings differ at small data is not that GeoTransolver fails on cases of
its own: its error barely varies by case at all. At 35 cases the
coefficient of variation of GeoTransolver's per-case error is 0.15 against
ISLA's 0.44, and at 210 cases 0.19 against 0.64; both models' errors rise
with angle of attack (rank correlation 0.56 and 0.61 at 35 cases), and
neither tracks how far a case's field is from uniform
(results/hilift_error_drivers_2026-09-07.json). On these random splits
the physical-drive GeoTransolver at small data is a nearly case-independent
predictor, which is what @sec-de-strata reads from the reference predictors
(on the geometry-poor ladder splits of @sec-de-strata its error does vary
by case, with coefficient of variation 0.27–0.41, and correlates with
ISLA's at 0.77; results/hilift_geo_percase_correlation_2026-09-08.json).
The input scale explains the flatness: with its global-context projector
collapsed to about one slice per head by the 2,679.5 in/s freestream
(@sec-de-unit-drive), GeoTransolver could not use the geometry it was
shown, and a nearly case-independent error is what a model with a
mis-scaled global input produces. ISLA's error varies three to four times
more across cases because it has learned the case-to-case physics — a
statement about ISLA that stands — and a model that has cannot be
rank-correlated with one that has not. The per-case structure of the
unit-drive baselines is not yet measured (@sec-program-status).

A third seed at 35 cases gives ISLA 0.138, GeoTransolver 0.359 and Transolver
0.409. ISLA's third seed falls inside its two-seed range (0.135–0.141);
GeoTransolver's falls below its range (0.375–0.409) and Transolver's just
above (0.398–0.406). The three-seed means are 0.138, 0.381 and 0.404, for
factors of 2.8x and 2.9x. At 210 cases the third seed gives ISLA 0.0657
and Transolver 0.0875, each inside its two-seed range, and GeoTransolver
0.107, far below its two-seed range of 0.157–0.160: GeoTransolver's three
seeds at 210 cases span a factor of 1.5 (0.107–0.160) where ISLA's and
Transolver's span 1.07. The three-seed means are 0.0648, 0.141 and 0.087,
for factors of 2.2x and 1.3x, and those are the 210-case physical-drive
factors this book states (results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json). The
physical-drive GeoTransolver's small-data results on this dataset are
seed-fragile in a way the other two architectures' are not, which fits its
flat, geometry-blind error at these sizes (@tbl-hilift-percase-rho): which
basin the optimizer lands in matters more than which cases it sees. That,
too, follows the input: under the unit drive GeoTransolver's two 35-case
seeds agree to 0.001 (0.124 and 0.125; @tbl-unit-drive).

## Where the physical-drive gap lives {#sec-de-strata}

The analyses of this section were designed to locate an ISLA advantage on
the validation set; what they located was the physical-drive gap, whose
object turned out to be the baselines' input scale (@sec-de-unit-drive).
They remain the record of where that gap sat, and the statements they make
about ISLA's own error distribution stand on their own. Two hypotheses
about a small-data gap make different predictions about where on the
validation set it appears. If it came from memorizing geometries, it should
collapse on validation geometries that the 35 training cases never contain;
if it came from interpolating angle of attack, it should collapse at the
one angle (18°) the training set lacks. The table stratifies the 35-case
results by both.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-strata
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
st = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json"))
print("| angle of attack [deg] | training cases at this angle | validation cases | ISLA | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for aoa in sorted(st["by_aoa"], key=int):
    r = st["by_aoa"][aoa]
    bold = "**" if r["n_train"] == 0 else ""
    print(f"| {bold}{aoa}{bold} | {r['n_train']} | {r['n_val']} | {r['mt2']:.3f} | {r['gt']:.3f} | {r['transolver']:.3f} | {r['gt']/r['mt2']:.1f} |")
print()
print(": The 35-case models stratified by angle of attack: geometric-mean pressure rel-L2 over the validation cases at each angle (both seeds). The 18° row (bold) is an angle absent from the 35 training cases. GeoTransolver and Transolver are the physical-drive models; see @sec-de-unit-drive. Data: results/hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-strata}")
print()
print("| validation geometry seen in training at another angle | validation cases | ISLA | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, lab in (("True", "yes"), ("False", "**no**")):
    r = st["by_geometry_seen"][k]
    print(f"| {lab} | {r['n_val']} | {r['mt2']:.3f} | {r['gt']:.3f} | {r['transolver']:.3f} | {r['gt']/r['mt2']:.1f} |")
print()
print(": The same models stratified by whether the validation geometry appears among the 33 geometries of the 35-case training set. Data: results/hilift_stratified_35_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-strata-geo}")
```

Neither collapse happens in the physical-drive gap. On the 146 validation
cases whose geometry is absent from the 35 training cases (146 cases on 96
geometries; results/hilift_seen_vs_unseen_geometry_2026-09-07.json) ISLA
is 3.0x ahead of the physical-drive baselines; seeing a geometry at another
angle helps ISLA by 15% and the physical-drive GeoTransolver not at all,
and at 210 cases that GeoTransolver is again identical on seen and unseen
geometries (0.158 against 0.159) while ISLA no longer needs to have seen
one (0.066 against 0.061;
results/hilift_seen_vs_unseen_geometry_2026-09-07.json). Together with the
per-case decorrelation of @tbl-hilift-percase-rho, this shows that the
physical-drive GeoTransolver did not exploit the geometries it had seen,
which the input scale explains: with its global-context projector collapsed
by the freestream magnitude (@sec-de-unit-drive), it could not use the
geometry at all. At 18°, ISLA interpolates smoothly between its 16° and 20°
errors (0.135 → 0.167 → 0.186), a statement about ISLA alone, and stays 2.5x
ahead of the physical-drive baselines. The gap is uniform — 2.2x to 4.3x at
every angle — and largest in attached flow (4°–12°), where ISLA's error is
0.09–0.10 against 0.33–0.39 for the physical-drive baselines; a gap that is
uniform across strata is what a baseline with a stratum-independent error
produces.

The strictest version of the geometry question removes the seen geometries
altogether. Trained on 40 cases made of only four geometries at all ten
angles, and validated on the 180 cases of 18 geometries that appear in no
training set at any angle, ISLA reaches 0.248 and 0.251 (two seeds) against
the physical-drive GeoTransolver's 0.407 and 0.492: 1.8x on pressure, 1.9x
on velocity, 1.7x on wall shear, and 172 of 180 cases (158 on both seeds; median per-case ratio
2.24; results/w2_reduction_2026-09-07b.json,
results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-07b.json). On this split the 180
validation cases are 18 geometries at ten angles each, so the independent
unit is the geometry and the case-win count is descriptive: with the paired
test that matches the design, ISLA is more accurate on 18 of 18 geometries
(the smallest attainable two-sided p at n = 18, 7.6e-6), the geometry-level
ratio has median 2.16 and 10–90% range 1.36–3.12, and a bootstrap over
geometries puts the ratio of mean errors at 1.56–2.16 (95%), wider than the
case-level 1.70–1.92 (results/hilift_paired_stats_geometry_2026-09-08.json).
Two things in these
numbers matter beyond the ratio. ISLA's error nearly doubles relative to the
35-case random split (0.138 → 0.250) when the number of distinct training
geometries falls from 33 to 4 at a similar case count, so its accuracy is
paid for in geometries, not cases; the physical-drive GeoTransolver's error
barely changes (0.39 → 0.45) and its two seeds disagree by 20%. That
comparison changes two things at once, the training composition and the
evaluation population (the random-split and geometry-ladder validation sets
share only 20 of 180 cases), so it supports a geometry-generalization
reading of the physical-drive gap and not the stronger statement that
geometry count alone sets ISLA's error. The 210-case rung of the same
ladder (21 geometries at all ten angles) repeats the pattern: ISLA 0.100
and 0.103 against the physical-drive GeoTransolver's 0.153 and 0.132, a
1.40x gap on pressure (1.37x velocity, 1.34x wall shear), where the random
210-case split with about 126 geometries gives 0.065 against 0.141: with
the same caveat, cutting the training geometries six-fold costs ISLA 1.6x
and the physical-drive GeoTransolver nothing; ISLA wins 172 of the 180
validation cases at this rung too (157 on both seeds, median per-case ratio
1.48; results/hilift_paired_stats_case_2026-09-08.json), and again 18 of 18
geometries, with the ratio of mean errors at 1.28–1.54 (95%, geometry
bootstrap; results/hilift_paired_stats_geometry_2026-09-08.json). The
measurement on never-seen geometries stands: 172 of 180 cases and 18 of 18
geometries at both rungs, against the physical-drive GeoTransolver. The
inference that ISLA generalizes across wing geometries where GeoTransolver
does not does not stand, because the unit-drive control removed a larger
deficit at 35 cases (@tbl-unit-drive); the unit-drive GeoTransolver at 4
and 21 training geometries decided these rungs (@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg). At
21 geometries it scores 0.0933 in float32 (seeds 0.0965 / 0.0900) against
ISLA's 0.1014, a ratio of 0.92 with GeoTransolver lower on 136 of 180
validation cases, inside the preregistered band between parity and
"baseline ahead" on the baseline's side; the physical-drive GeoTransolver
scores 0.142 in float32 on the same cases, 1.48x behind ISLA by the median
case, so the 1.40x was the input scale
(`results/udrvl_geo210_reduction_2026-09-10.json`, @sec-nb-udrvl-geo210-verdict).
Transolver fed the unit direction scores 0.0941 at this rung (0.93x of ISLA,
lower on 135 of 180 cases, the same band as GeoTransolver), and the
weights-off ablation of ISLA 0.0905 (0.89x of the weighted model, lower on
146 of 180), which prices the measure semantics at 11% here and puts the
ablation at parity with both unit-drive baselines; it is not adopted
(@sec-principle, `results/geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json`, @sec-nb-geo210-arms-verdict).
What stands about ISLA alone is that its error responds to the number of
training geometries (0.138 → 0.250 and 0.065 → 0.102, with the
evaluation-population caveat above); that the physical-drive
GeoTransolver's did not is what a collapsed global-context projector
predicts.

With the unit-drive GeoTransolver in place of the physical-drive one on the
same four-geometry split, the factor reverses by the mean and vanishes by
the count: the unit-drive GeoTransolver scores 0.189 (seeds 0.1888 /
0.1888) against ISLA's 0.250, a ratio of 0.76 (ISLA behind by the mean),
while per case it is lower on 96 of 180 and per geometry on 9 of 18, with a
median per-geometry ratio of 1.03 and a 10–90% range of 0.78–2.06
(results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09c.json, arm `gt_unit_geo40`;
@sec-nb-udrvl-geo40-verdict). The mean difference comes from a tail of
geometries where ISLA is up to twice as bad; on half of the held-out
geometries ISLA is the more accurate model. Neither bar of the ladder
preregistration for an ISLA advantage (≥ 1.10 and two thirds of the cases)
is approached, so "ISLA generalizes across wing geometries from few
samples" does not survive at four training geometries; its 1.8x was the
input scale (the unit-drive GeoTransolver is 2.4x more accurate than its
physical-drive twin, on 180 of 180 cases).

The strata also show *what kind* of model each physical-drive baseline was
at 35 cases, and what kind ISLA is. The physical-drive baselines' error is
nearly flat — 0.33 to 0.47 at every angle, identical on seen and unseen
geometries — while ISLA's tracks the physics, doubling from attached flow
to post-stall. Against reference predictors on the same cases (a constant
freestream pressure everywhere scores 1.00 on the gauge-pressure scale, the
dataset mean 0.94, each case's own mean 0.93), the physical-drive
GeoTransolver scores 0.63 and Transolver 0.68 while ISLA scores 0.25; the
median per-case correlation between predicted and true pressure is 0.76
and 0.69 for those baselines against 0.97 for ISLA
^[`results/hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json`]. At 35 cases the
physical-drive baselines had learned the coarse, case-independent pressure
pattern and about half of the case-to-case variation, which is what a model
whose global input is mis-scaled by three orders of magnitude produces
(@sec-de-unit-drive); ISLA has learned most of it, and that statement about
ISLA stands.

## In engineering terms: lift and drag {#sec-de-forces}

Integrating the predicted pressure and wall shear over each wing gives
its lift and drag coefficients. The table reports the mean absolute error
of each coefficient over the 180 validation cases, relative to the mean
magnitude of the reference coefficient (the recipe integrates with a unit
reference area, so only relative errors are meaningful). The reference is
the CFD label integrated on the *same* 10,000 sampled cells as the
prediction (@sec-metrics): the errors below are against that sampled-cell
integral, not against the full-surface force, and because prediction and
label share the quadrature, the sampling error of a 10,000-cell integral
cancels in them. How far a 10,000-cell integral sits from the full-surface
force is not yet measured (@sec-program-status).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-forces
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path
ps = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json"))
names = {"mt2": "ISLA", "gt": "GeoTransolver", "transolver": "Transolver (lr 3e-3)"}
print("| training cases | architecture | drag coefficient error | lift coefficient error |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for n in ("35", "210", "1260"):
    for a in ("mt2", "gt", "transolver"):
        f = ps[n]["forces"].get(a)
        if not f:
            continue
        b = "**" if a == "mt2" and n == "35" else ""
        print(f"| {int(n):,} | {names[a]} | {b}{100*f['CD']['rel_mae']:.1f}%{b} | {b}{100*f['CL']['rel_mae']:.1f}%{b} |")
print()
print(": Force-coefficient error: mean absolute error of the integrated drag (CD) and lift (CL) coefficients over the 180 validation cases, as a percentage of the mean magnitude of the true coefficient, averaged over seeds. GeoTransolver and Transolver are the physical-drive models; see @sec-de-unit-drive. Data: results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json. {#tbl-hilift-forces}")
```

From 35 CFD runs, ISLA predicts the lift and drag of unseen high-lift
configurations to about 3% of the sampled-cell reference; that is a number
about ISLA and it stands. The physical-drive GeoTransolver reached 11–17%
and the physical-drive Transolver 8–12%, so the comparison in the table is
a physical-drive comparison: the unit-drive baselines, which beat ISLA on
pressure and wall shear at 35 cases (@tbl-unit-drive), have no force
integration in this chapter. At 210 runs all three models of the
physical-drive ladder are within 1.5–3%, and at 1,260 the two-seed means
are indistinguishable. The 3% figure is the practical content of this section:
a few-dozen-run design-of-experiments budget yields a force surrogate of
usable accuracy from ISLA. It is not a claim that ISLA is the only
architecture that delivers one.

## Steel-man controls {#sec-de-controls}

A small-data gap can be a protocol artefact, and this one was
(@sec-de-unit-drive). The four GeoTransolver controls of this section
tested two other candidate artefacts, optimization budget and learning
rate: the fixed 500-epoch budget gives a 35-case model only 4,500 optimizer
steps, and the learning rate was chosen on the full split. Each control
kept the physical-velocity input, with the preregistered falsifier that any
control within 1.2x of ISLA at 35 cases voids the result.

| training cases | GeoTransolver control | error (seed 42 / seed 43) | GeoTransolver at the protocol rate and epochs | falsifier (1.2x ISLA) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs | 0.392 / 0.480 | 0.375 / 0.409 | 0.166 |
| 35 | learning rate 1e-3, 1,000 epochs | 0.373 / 0.429 | 0.375 / 0.409 | 0.166 |
| 210 | learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs | 0.220 / 0.290 | 0.157 / 0.160 | 0.077 |
| 210 | learning rate 1e-3, 1,000 epochs | 0.152 / 0.128 | 0.157 / 0.160 | 0.077 |

: GeoTransolver steel-man controls, two seeds each, on the shared validation set. A higher learning rate hurts at both rungs; doubling the epochs helps only at 210 cases (0.140 against 0.159, 1.13x) and leaves GeoTransolver 2.2x behind ISLA there. The doubled-epoch lanes kept the
protocol's step schedule (÷10 every 100 epochs), so their extra 500 epochs ran at a
learning rate of 10⁻⁶ or less; they test a longer low-rate tail, not a doubled
optimization budget, and the 210-case improvement is within their seed spread.
No control approaches the falsifier. All four controls kept the physical-velocity input; see @sec-de-unit-drive. Data: results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json. {#tbl-hilift-controls}

The same-family baseline (Transolver at its better learning rate) is a
further control, already in the tables above, and it too received the
physical velocity. A learning-rate explanation is also implausible on
independent grounds: GeoTransolver's sensitivity to learning rate is itself
one of the measured differences between the architectures
(@sec-robustness-lr).

These controls varied what the optimizer was given and could not find an
artefact in what the model was fed: every one of them kept the mis-scaled
input. The control that changed only the input is the one that found it,
taking GeoTransolver from 0.381 to 0.124 at 35 cases, far past the 0.166
falsifier that none of the controls here approached (@tbl-unit-drive). The
protocol rule this leaves is stated in @sec-de-limits.

## A free uncertainty signal {#sec-de-uq}

The disagreement between a model's two seeds ranks its per-case error at
35 cases for ISLA (Spearman +0.67 over the 180 validation cases) and not
for the physical-drive baselines (−0.20 and −0.47), at 210 cases for all
three (+0.60 to +0.65), and for none at 1,260 (+0.15 to +0.19); two-seed
ensembles gain only 1–5% at any rung, and only the ranking is tested, not
calibration.^[`results/hilift_ensemble_uq_{35,210,1260}_2026-09-06.json`.]
A two-seed ISLA therefore ships with a usable per-case confidence flag from
35 cases; that is a property of ISLA and it stands. The baselines' negative
correlations at 35 cases are those of the physical-drive models, whose
nearly flat per-case error (@sec-de-paired) leaves little to rank, and the
signal has not been measured on the unit-drive baselines, so no comparison
with them is made. The collapse at 1,260 cases is part of the shared-floor
evidence of @sec-shared-floor.

## What carried the physical-drive gap {#sec-mechanism}

This section asked which ingredient of ISLA carried its margin over the
baselines. The unit-drive control answered from the other side of the
comparison: the object of the physical-drive gap was the baselines' input
scale (@sec-de-unit-drive). The ISLA-side ablations below remain valid
measurements of ISLA's ingredients against ISLA's own reference; the
baseline-side tests, the fixed-angle split and the gap-region analysis are
analyses of the physical-drive gap and read as such.

ISLA differs from the Transolver family in several ways at once: exact
rotation and translation equivariance, an invariant seed parameterization,
measure-weighted routing, equivariant slice anchors with relational
invariants, and an optional similarity gauge. Removing one at a time at
35 cases (reference ISLA error 0.138) gives:

| single-factor change to ISLA at 35 cases | error (seed 42 / 43) | vs reference |
|---|---|---|
| add raw coordinates as inputs (breaks exact equivariance) | 0.143 / 0.143 | 1.04x |
| replace the invariant seeds by the raw vectors [r, n, d] | 0.138 / 0.137 | 0.99x |
| similarity gauge on | 0.151 / 0.147 | 1.08x |
| measure weights off | 0.121 / 0.123 | **0.88x** |
| relational routing off in the encoder | 0.158 / 0.163 | 1.16x |

: Single-factor ablations of ISLA at 35 training cases, two seeds, frozen protocol, shared validation set. Every variant retains an invariant path somewhere (the relational invariants in the encoder, or in the decoder read blocks), so these results speak to exactness and to individual ingredients, not to the presence of invariant information. Data: results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-05.json. {#tbl-hilift-ablations}

No single ingredient moves ISLA's error by more than 16%, against a 190%
physical-drive gap to the baselines that sat on the other side of the
comparison (@sec-de-unit-drive). Exactness of the
equivariance is not load-bearing (adding raw coordinates costs 4%); the
invariant seed set is not (raw vectors cost nothing); the gauge is neutral
to slightly harmful at this rung; and measure weights, which buy
sampling-density robustness (@sec-robustness-density), *cost* 12% at 35
cases; whether that cost is estimator variance or the loss of a non-physical
density signal is the open question of @sec-principle, and the weights stay
on regardless. Relational routing is worth 16%.

The complementary test from the baseline side gives GeoTransolver and
Transolver ISLA's three drive-relative invariants (local incidence n·d,
radial cosine, radius) as per-cell input features at 35 cases, with bands
fixed in advance: the inputs carry the gap if both baselines reach 0.235
or better (halfway to ISLA in log-error), and do not if both stay at 0.30
or worse. Transolver improves from 0.402 to 0.297 (a 1.35x gain, a quarter
of the log-gap, inside the inconclusive band); GeoTransolver does not move
(0.392 to 0.394, in the falsifier band). The invariant inputs are therefore
not the carrier for GeoTransolver and at most a partial contributor for
Transolver.^[`results/inv_transplant_2026-09-07.json`] The transplant kept
the physical velocity as the global input, so both baselines carried the
artefact through the test; the one baseline-side change that closes the
gap is the drive scale (@sec-de-unit-drive).

The single-angle split, rerun with unit-drive baselines, reverses the
fixed-angle figure. The dataset's `single_aoa_12` split holds 126 geometries
at one angle of attack (12°) and validates on 18 geometries never seen at
any angle. Against the physical-drive GeoTransolver (0.175 / 0.183) ISLA's
0.035 / 0.036 had read as a 5.0x advantage on 18 of 18 held-out geometries;
against the same GeoTransolver fed the unit freestream direction, and
nothing else changed, the figure is **0.81x** in bfloat16 and 0.78x in
float32 (@sec-nb-fp32-all-regrade): the unit-drive
GeoTransolver scores 0.029 / 0.029 (mean 0.0291) and is more accurate than
ISLA on 18 of 18 geometries (median per-geometry ISLA ÷ GeoTransolver 1.24,
10–90% range 1.06–1.36; exact sign test on 18 geometries p = 8 × 10⁻⁶), and
the unit-drive Transolver 0.032 / 0.032 (mean 0.0317), also 18 of 18
(median 1.13, range 1.06–1.21). Both unit-drive baselines lead ISLA on
velocity (0.053 and 0.059 against 0.065) and wall shear (0.087 and 0.097
against 0.106) as well. The weights-off ablation of ISLA (not adopted,
@sec-principle) scores 0.031 here in float32 (two seeds 0.032 / 0.030, against 0.035 with
the weights on; lower on 17 of 18 geometries), which closes a third of the
deficit to the unit-drive GeoTransolver (0.87x of the weights-off ISLA,
GeoTransolver lower on 18 of 18) and brings Transolver into the parity band
(0.96x, Transolver lower on 14 of 18); ISLA remains behind both
(`results/now_single12_reduction_2026-09-10.json`, @sec-nb-now-single12-verdict). The physical-drive GeoTransolver is 6.2x worse than
its unit-drive twin on every geometry
(results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09b.json, arms `gt_unit_single12`,
`transolver_unit_single12`; preregistered bars in @sec-nb-udrv-prereg,
verdict @sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict). That ISLA reaches 0.036 from 126
single-angle cases, with lift to 0.6% and drag to 1.6% against the
sampled-cell label integral (@sec-de-forces), is a statement about ISLA and
stands; the reading it once invited, that ISLA generalizes across high-lift
geometries where GeoTransolver from 126 geometries at one operating point
has not begun to, is falsified: GeoTransolver with a usable drive input
generalizes across the same geometries better than ISLA does. The
mixed-angle control (126 cases at all angles: ISLA 0.077, physical-drive
GeoTransolver 0.226) and the Transolver decomposition of the fixed-angle
gap (physical-drive Transolver 0.091, 1.96x ahead of physical-drive
GeoTransolver and 2.55x behind ISLA) are measurements of the physical-drive
protocol and no longer bear on the architectures
(results/w2_reduction_2026-09-08b.json); the part of the old gap common to
both baselines, 2.5x, was the input scale, as the unit-drive rerun shows. The
DrivAerML contrast — GeoTransolver 1.2–1.3x ahead on smooth single-body
morphs of one car — needs no geometry-variation mechanism; GeoTransolver's
DrivAerML lanes also received the physical velocity, so its lead there is a
lower bound (@sec-de-drivaerml). The remaining physical-drive figures on
held-out geometries are in @sec-de-strata (1.8x from four training
geometries, 1.40x from 21), with their unit-drive reruns training; a
GeoTransolver learning-rate steel-man at the single angle, which kept the
physical velocity, made GeoTransolver worse (0.280 at 3e-3 against 0.179 at
1e-3; results/w2_reduction_2026-09-08.json), which is what a steel-man that
holds the decisive variable fixed produces.

**The alternative on the baseline side of the protocol is the one that
holds.** GeoTransolver and Transolver receive the freestream as a physical
velocity, 2,679.5 in/s on HiLiftAeroML and 38.9 m/s on DrivAerML, where
ISLA receives a unit direction; at initialization that magnitude collapses
GeoTransolver's global-context slice occupancy from about 200 effective
slices per head to about one (@sec-part-baseline). The training control
that swaps the velocity for the unit direction with everything else frozen
removes the 35-case deficit entirely (@sec-de-unit-drive); the transplant
test above kept the raw velocity, which is why it could not.

**The small-feature hypothesis, tested where it can be tested on the
physical-drive checkpoints, does not place the gap where it predicts.** A
high-lift wing differs from its neighbours in the family in
the slat and flap deflections and, through them, in the gaps between
elements: geometric features a few percent of the chord in size, covered
by a few dozen of the 10,000 sampled points each, which set the pressure
over the whole element downstream of them. A DrivAerML car differs from its
neighbours by a smooth morph of one body, with no such features. If ISLA's
relational routing resolves small geometric features from few samples where
GeoTransolver's geometry encoder does not, the prediction was that ISLA's
*error* margin over GeoTransolver concentrates on the gap regions and is
smaller elsewhere. The test is eval-only on the physical-drive checkpoints.
HiLiftAeroML carries no
element labels and each CFD boundary mesh is one connected body (the slats
and flaps are joined to the wing through brackets and fairings), so the
preregistered partition by connected component is not available; the gap
regions are defined geometrically instead, by the *facing-surface
distance*: from each sampled point, the distance to the nearest
boundary-mesh vertex in front of the surface within 10% of chord, which is
the local gap or cove width and is infinite on an open convex surface
(@sec-nb-hlreg-amendment). The bands are 0.7–2%, 2–10% and above 10% of
chord; the near band holds about 15% of the points.

| training cases | near band (0.7–2% chord) | 2–10% | open surface (>10%) | near ÷ rest | ISLA's error share in the near band | GeoTransolver's |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | 2.01 | 2.02 | 3.00 | 0.72 (0.38–1.31) | 59% | 33% |
| 210 | 1.87 | 2.76 | 2.57 | 0.78 (0.54–1.09) | 71% | 56% |

: GeoTransolver/ISLA RMS pressure-error ratio by facing-surface-distance band,
against physical-drive GeoTransolver (see @sec-de-unit-drive)
(two-seed mean predictions, median over the 180 validation cases; the
near-over-rest column gives its 10th–90th percentiles), and each model's
share of its own squared error that falls in the near band. Preregistered
bars (@sec-nb-hlreg-prereg): supported if near ÷ rest ≥ 1.5 at 35 cases,
falsified if within 0.87–1.15. Data:
results/hlreg_facing_distance_35_2026-09-08.json,
results/hlreg_facing_distance_210_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-hilift-hlreg}

The prediction is falsified, and in the opposite direction: the
physical-drive gap is *smallest* in the gap regions (2.0x and 1.9x) and
largest on the open surfaces at 35 cases (3.0x), with 61% of cases below the
0.87 floor of the "uniform" band and 7% above the 1.5 bar; the ordering is
the same at 210 cases. What the bands do show is where each model's residual
error lives: 59% of ISLA's squared error at 35 cases, and 71% at 210, falls
on the 15% of points in the gap regions — a statement about ISLA that stands
— against 33% and 56% for the physical-drive GeoTransolver, whose error is
spread over the open surfaces. Both models find the gaps hardest; the
physical-drive gap is widest where the pressure field is smooth, which is
where a nearly case-independent predictor (@sec-de-paired) is furthest from
the truth. One limit on what this can say, stated before the result
(@sec-nb-hlreg-prereg): the instrument locates where the *output* error
differs, not where the *input* information that drives it lives. A change
of slat gap alters circulation and hence pressure over the whole element, so
this result does not exclude the idea that gap geometry is what ISLA reads
better from few samples; it excludes the prediction that the resulting error
margin sits at the gaps. The information question needs a perturbation test
(gap-region points removed or perturbed against matched-area controls, on a
fixed query set), which is a separate node (@sec-program-status) and is
worth running only if a gap survives the unit-drive rerun.

## The same protocol on DrivAerML {#sec-de-drivaerml}

There is no ISLA advantage on DrivAerML at any training-set size. Its
data-efficiency ladder (@sec-datasets) trains both architectures on nested
subsets of the 435-car training split — 14, 27, 54, 109 and 218 cars —
under the frozen protocol of that ladder, learning rate 3e-3 for both, 500
epochs, 10,000 tokens, two seeds, scored on the 48-car validation split.
GeoTransolver's DrivAerML lanes also received the freestream as a physical
velocity, 38.9 m/s; at 435 cars the unit-drive rerun scores 0.0503 against
0.0498 in float32 (0.0556 against 0.0548 in bfloat16), inside the null
band, so on this dataset the input scale is not a handicap and the table's
ladder ordering is read as it stands (@sec-nb-uw-verdict,
@sec-nb-fp32-drivaer-regrade).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "ladder_reduction.json"))
print("| training cars | GeoTransolver | ISLA | GT / ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|")
for n in (14, 27, 54, 109, 218):
    g = [lad[f"lad_gt_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    m = [lad[f"lad_mt2_n{n}_seed{s}"]["infamily"] for s in (42, 43)]
    gm, mm = statistics.mean(g), statistics.mean(m)
    print(f"| {n} | {gm:.3f} ({min(g):.3f}–{max(g):.3f}) | {mm:.3f} ({min(m):.3f}–{max(m):.3f}) | {gm/mm:.2f} |")
print()
print(": DrivAerML data-efficiency ladder: surface-pressure relative L2 on the 48 validation cars, seed mean (seed range), at learning rate 3e-3 for both architectures (the frozen protocol of that ladder; ISLA's preferred rate of 1e-3 is worth about 1.1x at full data and does not change the ordering). GT / ISLA below one means GeoTransolver is more accurate. Data: results/ladder_reduction.json. {#tbl-drivaerml-dataeff-ladder}")
```

At 14 cars the two architectures tie at 0.27; from 27 cars up GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate, a gap that
persists to the full split (1.085x at each architecture's best rate,
@sec-full-data). The HiLift physical-drive gap does not recur here even
though GeoTransolver received the physical velocity on both datasets; the
magnitudes differ by a factor of about 70, and GeoTransolver's
global-context projector at initialization collapses to 1.0–3.8 effective
slices per head at 38.9 where at 2,679.5 it collapses to about one
(results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json), so the two
datasets did not receive the same artefact. The same 1.2x appears on the
interior: trained on 54 cars, GeoTransolver's volume configuration leads
ISLA's query-token configuration by 1.21x on interior pressure, and the two
reach parity only at 435 cars (@sec-interior). On DrivAerML the deficit is
uniform in every way measured: the same on every third of the car
(@sec-limits-mechanism), a near-constant factor per car on a difficulty
ordering both architectures share (@tbl-hilift-percase-rho), unchanged by a
wider ISLA, and the same for the surface and the volume. How much of
GeoTransolver's DrivAerML lead the unit drive would add is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status).

## Limits of the claim {#sec-de-limits}

**The comparison had an input-scale artefact, and the program's own
controls did not find it.** The baselines received the freestream as a
physical velocity of 2,679.5 in/s and ISLA a unit direction; retrained with
the unit direction and nothing else changed, GeoTransolver and Transolver
are 1.1–1.25x more accurate than ISLA at 35 cases (@sec-de-unit-drive). Four
steel-man controls (@sec-de-controls), a same-family baseline, a third seed,
an invariant-input transplant and a learning-rate steel-man at the fixed
angle all kept the input and all left the gap standing; an external audit of
the recipe configurations found the asymmetry by reading them. The protocol
rule that follows, and that the fair-comparison protocol now carries
(@sec-protocol): every input each architecture receives is listed with its
scale, the scales are matched across architectures, and a control that
varies only the input is part of the steel-man set before any ratio is
stated. Every physical-drive ratio above 35 cases in this chapter is
conditional on the unit-drive rerun (@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg).

**The physical-drive ladder is a data-efficiency measurement, not a
scaling law.** The measured log-log slopes of error against training cases,
fitted on the two-seed means, are 0.50 then 0.74 for the physical-drive
GeoTransolver and 0.43 then 0.25 for ISLA over the 35→210 and 210→1,260
segments (on the three-seed means the GeoTransolver segments are 0.553 and
0.675; results/hilift_slopes_threeseed_2026-09-08.json): GeoTransolver's
curve steepens where ISLA's flattens, and a naive power-law extrapolation
of the two curves puts GeoTransolver at 0.015 and ISLA at 0.029 at 5,000
cases, a factor of two in GeoTransolver's favour. The book makes no claim
beyond 1,260 cases. Three pieces of evidence suggest the flattening is a
shared floor of the protocol rather than a property of ISLA — 70% of the
residual at full data is shared between the two architectures on identical
points, the seed-disagreement correlation collapses for both at 1,260
cases, and accuracy still rises with tokens per case — but that reading is
a hypothesis under test (both architectures at 1,260 cases with 20,000
tokens), not a result (@sec-shared-floor).

**It is one dataset, and on the other the ordering is GeoTransolver's.** On
DrivAerML GeoTransolver is 1.2–1.3x more accurate from 27 training cases up
and the two tie at 14 (@sec-de-drivaerml), with GeoTransolver also fed the
physical velocity there. At 35 HiLift cases the contrast between the two
datasets is accounted for by the input scale rather than by anything ISLA
represents; the transplant of drive-relative features to the baselines did
not close the gap because it kept the velocity (@sec-mechanism).

**It is in-distribution, and it is a validation-set figure.** The
validation cases are random draws from the same 180-geometry, ten-angle
design as the training cases (180 cases on 118 geometries); the checkpoints
are final-epoch, with no selection on validation error, but the validation
set was reused adaptively (Transolver's rate per rung, the ablations
designed after earlier readouts, the choice of what to present), and the
sealed test split has been spent on regime extrapolation and one mechanism
test, so no held-out evaluation of the 35-case models exists. Nor can one
now be an independent confirmation at the level of the program: the
regime-extrapolation test sets cover all 180 geometries and share 179 of
the 360 data-efficiency test cases, so a later evaluation on that manifest
would be held out per checkpoint but not unexposed
(@sec-limits-validation). What happens
across a regime boundary is the subject of @sec-regime-extrapolation, and
the answer there is that no architecture generalizes.

**Seeds do not measure the choice of training cases.** Every seed at a rung
trains on the same curated subset, so the seed spread measures
initialization and data order, not which 35 cases (or which four
geometries) a practitioner would happen to have. The horizontal reading of
@tbl-data-multiplier is a comparison of two measured points, the
physical-drive GeoTransolver at 210 cases against ISLA at 35; it is not the
minimum number of CFD runs either architecture would need under a chosen
sampling of the design space, which would require repeated
geometry-stratified training draws that have not been run.

**No mechanism of an ISLA advantage is established, because no ISLA
advantage over an input-matched baseline is established.** The
geometry-generalization reading of @sec-de-strata and @sec-mechanism
describes the physical-drive gap, whose object was the baselines' input
scale. Should the unit-drive rerun leave a gap at any rung
(@sec-nb-udrvl-prereg), the question of which ingredient of ISLA carries it
reopens, with the single-factor ablations of @tbl-hilift-ablations (no
ingredient worth more than 16%) as the starting point.
